CausalChain: SF3B2 upregulation + SF3B1/SF3B4 co-dysregulation -> Aberrant splicing of TP53 and RAD51 -> Impaired DNA repair and altered chromatin environment -> Enhanced susceptibility to viral DNA integration (in presence of hepatotropic viruses) -> Genomic instability -> Activation of metastasis and angiogenesis -> Poor liver neoplasm prognosis
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in a subset of liver neoplasms, the overexpression of SF3B2, together with dysregulation of co-splicing factors SF3B1 and SF3B4, drives the creation of abnormal splice variants of DNA repair regulators (TP53 and RAD51). This splicing alteration impairs DNA repair mechanisms and remodels the chromatin to form a permissive environment for viral DNA integration—especially when hepatotropic viruses such as HBV or HCV are present. As viral genomes integrate more readily, genomic instability escalates, triggering oncogenic signaling pathways that promote metastasis and angiogenesis, and ultimately leading to adverse clinical outcomes. Our study will exploit a suite of modern technologies including high-throughput and single-cell RNA sequencing, CRISPR interference screens to modulate splicing factor levels, and long-read sequencing for precise mapping of viral integration sites, supplemented by functional assays to assess DNA repair capacity.
Abstract: We propose that in a subset of liver cancers, the coordinated overexpression of SF3B2, in synergy with SF3B1 and SF3B4, leads to the production of aberrant splice variants of key DNA repair regulators such as TP53 and RAD51. These mis-spliced forms compromise the efficiency of DNA repair and induce changes in the chromatin landscape, thereby establishing a cellular environment that is highly susceptible to viral DNA integration—particularly in the context of hepatotropic viruses like HBV and HCV. The resulting integration events further intensify genomic instability and activate oncogenic pathways linked to metastasis and angiogenesis, culminating in poorer clinical outcomes. We will leverage state-of-the-art technologies including high-throughput and single-cell RNA sequencing, CRISPR interference screening, functional DNA repair assays, and long-read sequencing to dissect the mechanistic links between splicing dysregulation, impaired DNA repair, viral integration, and liver tumor progression.
Orignal_vs_New: The revised hypothesis retains the original causal chain but refines the mechanism by: (1) explicitly conditioning the viral DNA integration step on the presence of hepatotropic viruses, addressing the gap regarding the trigger for integration events; (2) detailing the nature of the aberrant splice variants of TP53 and RAD51 to clarify their impact on DNA repair; and (3) incorporating additional functional assays and advanced sequencing technologies (including single-cell and long-read sequencing) to robustly test each step in the causal chain. These modifications enhance both the logical coherence and practical implementability of the hypothesis, while preserving its novel integration of splicing dysregulation and viral integration in liver oncogenesis.
